rebuttals.chipLabel: S1. Russia Broke Treaties Under Deterrence
rebuttals.trigger: If they say nuclear deterrence keeps Russia in check or makes Russia respect arms control:
rebuttals.response: Look at what Russia actually did while NATO's full nuclear deterrent was in place. NATO's own North Atlantic Council found Russia violated the INF Treaty with its 9M729 missile and 'bears sole responsibility for the demise of the Treaty' (NAC, 19). In February 2023 Putin announced 'Russia is suspending its participation' in New START (Bugos, 23), and in November 2023 he revoked Russia's ratification of the nuclear test ban (AP, 23). Deterrence did not keep Russia inside a single treaty. Why this matters for your ballot: their 'wait for Russia' world has already failed, while our case works through European law Moscow cannot veto.

rebuttals.chipLabel: S2. Putin's Nuclear Threats Happened Anyway
rebuttals.trigger: If they say Europe needs nuclear weapons to stop Russian nuclear blackmail or threats:
rebuttals.response: The blackmail they fear already happened with every NATO nuke in place. In February 2022, Putin put his nuclear forces in a 'special regime of combat duty' (AP, 22). In September 2022 he said 'This is not a bluff.' In November 2024 he signed a doctrine lowering the threshold for nuclear use (AP, 24), then fired the nuclear-capable Oreshnik at Dnipro (NPR, 24). Yet Scholz said nuclear use would 'cross a line that the international community has drawn together' (AP, 22). Why this matters for your ballot: nukes did not stop the threats; the TPNW writes that line into law.

rebuttals.chipLabel: S3. Trump: Umbrella Is Conditional (Target, Not Shield)
rebuttals.trigger: If they say the US nuclear umbrella and US B61 bombs keep Europe safe:
rebuttals.response: In March 2025 President Trump said, 'If they don't pay, I'm not going to defend them' (AP, 25). In June 2025, asked about Article 5, he said it 'depends on your definition' (AP, 25). His December 2025 strategy told Europe to take 'primary responsibility for its own defense' (White House NSS, 25), and in May 2026 the Pentagon announced about 5,000 troops leaving Germany (CNBC, 26). A conditional guarantee is a bluff, and a bluff stored at six European airbases (Kristensen, 26) is a target, not a shield. Why this matters for your ballot: their main harm needs a real umbrella, and their own guarantor says it isn't.
rebuttals.citation: AP, 25, White House NSS, 25, CNBC, 26 & Kristensen, 26

rebuttals.chipLabel: S4. UK & France Are Expanding, Not Disarming
rebuttals.trigger: If they say Britain and France are responsible, defensive nuclear powers that follow the rules:
rebuttals.response: The UK planned to cut its warhead ceiling to 180, then in 2021 announced it 'will move to an overall nuclear weapon stockpile of no more than 260 warheads' and stopped publishing operational numbers (UK Integrated Review, 21). In March 2026 Macron said 'I have decided to increase the number of warheads of our arsenal' and 'we will no longer release figures' (Macron, 26). Yet both signed NPT Article VI, promising to 'pursue negotiations in good faith' on 'cessation of the nuclear arms race at an early date' (NPT Text, 68). Why this matters for your ballot: the status quo is a growing, more secretive European arms race; the TPNW reverses it.
rebuttals.citation: UK Integrated Review, 21, Macron, 26 & NPT Text, 68

rebuttals.chipLabel: S5. China Proves Deterrence Fuels Arms Races
rebuttals.trigger: If they say nuclear deterrence prevents arms races, or that China's buildup proves Europe needs nukes:
rebuttals.response: China proves the opposite. Facing the two largest arsenals on Earth, China did not stop: the Pentagon's 2020 estimate was the 'low 200s', and its December 2025 report says the 'low 600s', on track to surpass 1,000 by 2030 (Defense News, 25). SIPRI says China is 'expanding its nuclear arsenal faster than any other country,' and SIPRI's Hans Kristensen warns that 'by reaching for nuclear solutions, states are creating new risks and fuelling arms-race dynamics' (SIPRI Yearbook, 26). Deterrence does not end races; it starts them. Why this matters for your ballot: more nukes in Europe means more nukes everywhere, so Con's world gets more dangerous every year.

rebuttals.chipLabel: S6. Consider the Source: NATO Grades Its Own Homework
rebuttals.trigger: If they cite NATO statements saying the TPNW is incompatible with NATO or undermines security:
rebuttals.response: NATO's 2022 Strategic Concept says 'As long as nuclear weapons exist, NATO will remain a nuclear alliance' (NATO Strategic Concept, 22), its statements need consensus from three nuclear-armed members, and in 2020 Washington urged countries to withdraw their TPNW ratifications (AP, 20). That's like asking a tobacco company whether smoking is safe. Independent lawyers disagree: NATO's former legal adviser notes the North Atlantic Treaty 'does not mention nuclear weapons' (Hill, 21), and Harvard's clinic finds a TPNW member can stay in NATO (Harvard Law Clinic, 18). Why this matters for your ballot: weigh independent legal analysis over policy statements from the side with a stake in the outcome.
rebuttals.citation: NATO Strategic Concept, 22, AP, 20, Hill, 21 & Harvard Law Clinic, 18

rebuttals.chipLabel: S7. Steadfast Noon 2026: Threat, Drill, Repeat
rebuttals.trigger: If they say NATO nuclear exercises like Steadfast Noon show strength and keep the peace:
rebuttals.response: Look at the timing. In late September 2026 Russia warned it 'would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons' over Kaliningrad; weeks later, on October 13, NATO launched Steadfast Noon with 17 countries in Italy (AP, 26; Stars and Stripes, 26). AP reports NATO's own nuclear policy chief acknowledged Russia's nuclear rhetoric is on the rise. Threat, drill, threat, drill: that is a spiral, not stability, and every turn is another chance for the kind of miscalculation Lewis, 14 documents. Why this matters for your ballot: the TPNW takes Europe out of the cycle instead of rehearsing it every October.

traps.trigger: They say nuclear deterrence keeps Russia in line.
traps.question: Since Russia suspended New START in February 2023 and revoked its nuclear test-ban ratification in November 2023, while NATO's full nuclear deterrent was in place, what exactly did NATO's nukes deter?

traps.trigger: They say European nukes stop Russian missile threats.
traps.question: Russia fired the nuclear-capable Oreshnik at Dnipro in November 2024 and again in western Ukraine in January 2026, which the EU's Kaja Kallas said was 'meant as a warning to Europe and to the U.S.' Did NATO's 100 B61 bombs stop either launch?

traps.trigger: They rely on Trump and the US umbrella.
traps.question: President Trump said, 'If they don't pay, I'm not going to defend them.' So is your nuclear umbrella a guarantee, or a subscription that can be canceled?

traps.trigger: They say the US keeps the nuclear order stable.
traps.question: On October 30, 2025, President Trump ordered the Pentagon 'to start testing our Nuclear Weapons on an equal basis.' If the country holding Europe's umbrella is talking about testing again, who is actually keeping the arms race in check: the umbrella, or a treaty that bans testing?

traps.trigger: They say Britain and France keep their NPT promises.
traps.question: The UK raised its warhead ceiling to 260 in 2021 and France announced more warheads in March 2026. Which part of NPT Article VI's promise to end 'the nuclear arms race at an early date' is that?
traps.source: UK Integrated Review, 21, Macron, 26 & NPT Text, 68

prefires.chip: S1. Trump Won't Defend → Own Nukes?
prefires.topicLabel: If Trump won't defend Europe, doesn't Europe need its own nukes or the French umbrella?
prefires.coreAnswer: No. If Trump's promise is shaky, that proves nuclear protection is a bluff you can't control, and 'let's get our own bombs' is exactly the proliferation the TPNW stops. France and Britain built their forces for their own survival: Macron himself said there will be 'no sharing of the ultimate decision' and 'no guarantee in the strict sense of the term' (Macron, 26), and CSIS found major obstacles to Anglo-French forces covering Eastern Europe (Horschig, 25). Ratifying keeps Article 5's conventional defense (Harvard Law Clinic, 18), where European NATO alone spends $559 billion to Russia's $190 billion (SIPRI, 26).
prefires.citation: Macron, 26 & Horschig, 25 & Harvard Law Clinic, 18 & SIPRI, 26

prefires.chip: S2. Trump Is Just Talk / Still in NATO
prefires.topicLabel: Aren't Trump's NATO comments just talk? He's still in NATO.
prefires.coreAnswer: Either way, we win. If it's just talk, then the US president is publicly treating the guarantee as negotiable, so it is a bluff Russia hears too; if it's real, Europe must defend itself with the conventional forces where it already outspends Russia (SIPRI, 26). And it isn't only talk: about 5,000 US troops are leaving Germany (CNBC, 26) and the Romania brigade went home without a replacement (Fox News, 25). Yes, the US is still in NATO, and US law bars a president from quitting without two-thirds of the Senate or an Act of Congress (22 USC 1928f, 23); that Article 5 alliance is exactly what Europe keeps under the TPNW (Harvard Law Clinic, 18).
prefires.citation: SIPRI, 26 & CNBC, 26 & Fox News, 25 & 22 USC 1928f, 23 & Harvard Law Clinic, 18

prefires.topicLabel: Without nuclear weapons, why would Russia believe NATO's Article 5?
prefires.coreAnswer: Article 5's credibility comes from soldiers, jets and money, not bombs: the North Atlantic Treaty 'does not mention nuclear weapons' (Hill, 21), and the 29 European allies spend $559 billion a year to Russia's $190 billion (SIPRI, 26). The B61s were already in Europe when President Trump said Article 5 'depends on your definition' (AP, 25), so the bombs never made the promise believable. TPNW members keep Article 5 conventional defense (Harvard Law Clinic, 18).
prefires.citation: Hill, 21 & SIPRI, 26 & AP, 25 & Harvard Law Clinic, 18

prefires.chip: S4. Poland & Baltics Want More Nukes
prefires.topicLabel: Poland and the Baltic states are asking for more nuclear protection, so why would they ratify?
prefires.coreAnswer: Frontline states are asking because the US promise is wobbling, which proves nuclear 'protection' is a bluff they can't control; even France's offer comes with 'no guarantee in the strict sense of the term' (Macron, 26). What actually protects Poland is troops and air defense, which is why Tusk paired his nuclear talk with a plan to grow the army to about half a million (Tusk, 25). Under this resolution Poland ratifies too, so TPNW Article 1 legally closes the door on a Polish bomb instead of leaving it open.

prefires.topicLabel: Germany's Chancellor Merz wants nuclear protection, so won't Germany go nuclear?
prefires.coreAnswer: Germany already promised the world it won't: in the 1990 Two Plus Four Treaty it reaffirmed its 'renunciation of the manufacture and possession of and control over nuclear, biological and chemical weapons' (Two Plus Four Treaty, 90), and NPT Article II bars it from acquiring them (NPT Text, 68). Merz himself told Munich that 'a chasm, a deep rift, has opened between Europe and the United States' (Merz, 26), so resting German security on a bomb Germany doesn't control is the riskier bet. The TPNW locks Germany's promise in and points its $114 billion budget (SIPRI, 26) at conventional defense.
prefires.citation: Two Plus Four Treaty, 90 & NPT Text, 68 & Merz, 26 & SIPRI, 26

prefires.topicLabel: How does Europe defend against Russia's Oreshnik missile without nukes?
prefires.coreAnswer: Oreshnik proves nukes in Europe don't stop Russian escalation: Russia fired it at Dnipro in November 2024 with what Putin said was a 'nonnuclear warhead' (NPR, 24), fired it again in western Ukraine in January 2026 (AP, 26), and put it on combat duty in Belarus in December 2025 (Al Jazeera, 25), all while about 100 US B61 bombs sat in Europe (Kristensen, 26). The answer to a missile is air and missile defense plus conventional deep strike (van Hooft, 25), not a gravity bomb that has to be flown into Russian air defenses.
prefires.citation: NPR, 24 & AP, 26 & Al Jazeera, 25 & Kristensen, 26 & van Hooft, 25

prefires.topicLabel: China is racing to build nukes, so isn't disarming Europe naive?
prefires.coreAnswer: China's buildup proves deterrence fuels arms races, not that Europe should join one: SIPRI estimates about 620 Chinese warheads and says China is growing 'faster than any other country' (SIPRI Yearbook, 26), even though it already faced the huge US and Russian arsenals. SIPRI also notes that even 1,000 Chinese warheads by 2030 would be 'only about one quarter' of the current US or Russian stockpile, and Europe's B61 bombs were never aimed at China. Shrinking the race means strengthening the global rule against nukes, which is what the TPNW does.

prefires.chip: S8. Arms Control Is Dead (New START)
prefires.topicLabel: With New START gone and arms control dead, isn't the TPNW pointless?
prefires.coreAnswer: Exactly the opposite: that collapse is the strongest reason to ratify. New START expired on February 5, 2026, leaving the US and Russia 'with no legally binding curbs' on deploying strategic weapons (Liang, 26), after Russia suspended its participation in 2023 (Bugos, 23). Two-country, deterrence-based arms control has failed; the TPNW is the one nuclear disarmament treaty still growing, with 75 states parties (Hiroshima TPNW Tracker, 26).

prefires.topicLabel: Russia cheats on every treaty, so why would this one work?
prefires.coreAnswer: Russia does cheat: NATO itself found Russia violated the INF Treaty with its 9M729 missile and 'bears sole responsibility for the demise of the Treaty' (NAC, 19). That's why our case never asks Russia to join or trusts Putin's word: the TPNW binds European democracies, whose compliance is checked through IAEA safeguards they already accept (Hill, 21). And notice Russia cheated while NATO had full nuclear deterrence, so nukes don't stop cheating either.

prefires.topicLabel: Russia lowered its nuclear threshold in 2024, so doesn't Europe need nuclear deterrence more?
prefires.coreAnswer: Russia's November 2024 doctrine proves deterrence isn't calming Moscow: Putin lowered his own threshold while NATO's full arsenal was in place, declaring that a conventional attack by a nation 'supported by a nuclear power' counts as a joint attack on Russia (AP, 24). A doctrine built on threats isn't talked down by more threats; it is isolated by the global rule against nuclear use and threats, which TPNW Article 1(1)(d) makes law. And NATO's conventional edge of $1.58 trillion to $190 billion (SIPRI, 26) means Europe never needs to cross that threshold.

prefires.chip: S11. Gives Trump an Excuse to Quit NATO?
prefires.topicLabel: Won't ratifying the TPNW give Trump an excuse to pull out of NATO?
prefires.coreAnswer: Trump's threats came before any TPNW vote, over spending, Iran and Greenland (AP, 25; CNBC, 26), so ratifying doesn't create that risk; it already exists. And US law says the President 'shall not' withdraw from the North Atlantic Treaty without two-thirds of the Senate or an Act of Congress (22 USC 1928f, 23). Norway and Denmark have refused nukes on their soil in peacetime for decades and remain NATO members (Defense News, 26).

prefires.chip: S12. Forward Deterrence Covers the East
prefires.topicLabel: Macron's forward deterrence now covers Eastern Europe, so isn't the French umbrella credible?
prefires.coreAnswer: Read Macron's own words: there will be 'no sharing of the definition of our vital interests,' which 'will remain of sovereign assessment for our country,' and 'no guarantee in the strict sense of the term' (Macron, 26). So a Baltic state gets a French president's case-by-case judgment, not a promise, and CSIS found major obstacles to Anglo-French forces covering Eastern Europe (Horschig, 25). That is weaker than the US guarantee Con already admits is shaky.

prefires.chip: S13. US Troops Leaving → Nukes Fill Gap
prefires.topicLabel: With US troops leaving Europe, doesn't Europe need nukes to fill the gap?
prefires.coreAnswer: Nukes can't fill a soldier gap. When about 5,000 US troops leave Germany (CNBC, 26) and the Romania brigade goes home without a replacement (Fox News, 25), what's missing is boots, air defense and ammunition, conventional things Europe can buy with $559 billion a year (SIPRI, 26). Threatening nuclear war over a border town is the least believable answer to a manpower problem (Shlapak, 16).

prefires.chip: S14. US Wants to Resume Testing
prefires.topicLabel: If even the US is moving to resume nuclear testing, why should Europe disarm?
prefires.coreAnswer: That's the arms race we're warning about. On October 30, 2025, Trump posted that he had told the Pentagon 'to start testing our Nuclear Weapons on an equal basis' (Reuters, 25), though the US hasn't tested since 1992 and his Energy Secretary later said the tests would not be nuclear explosions. When the umbrella-holder talks about testing, 30 European NATO members ratifying a treaty that bans nuclear testing strengthens the norm instead of cheering the race.

prefires.topicLabel: Why not just build an EU nuclear bomb instead?
prefires.coreAnswer: A Eurobomb would break the NPT: every non-nuclear EU state promised 'not to manufacture or otherwise acquire nuclear weapons' (NPT Text, 68), and Germany renewed that pledge in 1990 (Two Plus Four Treaty, 90). Building a new bomb because an ally wobbles is exactly how proliferation spreads, and SIPRI warns that leaning more on nuclear weapons 'could significantly increase nuclear risks' (SIPRI Yearbook, 26). Europe's real edge is conventional: $559 billion to Russia's $190 billion (SIPRI, 26).
prefires.citation: NPT Text, 68 & Two Plus Four Treaty, 90 & SIPRI Yearbook, 26 & SIPRI, 26

prefires.topicLabel: Polls show Europeans want their own nuclear deterrent, so shouldn't leaders listen?
prefires.coreAnswer: The same ECFR poll shows why: majorities in every country polled think 'the US would not support them if they came under attack' (ECFR, 26), so the umbrella has already failed in voters' eyes. A poll measuring fear is not a security strategy, and when asked about the TPNW itself, 77 to 89 percent in six NATO countries supported joining (ICAN, 21). Opinion swings; the risk of one nuclear mistake doesn't.

prefires.chip: S17. Didn't Nukes Stop Putin Using Nukes?
prefires.topicLabel: Didn't NATO's nukes stop Putin from actually using nuclear weapons in Ukraine?
prefires.coreAnswer: There's no proof NATO's bombs are what held Putin back, but there is proof the global norm mattered: after months of Russian threats, Xi Jinping called on the world to 'jointly oppose the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons,' and Scholz said nuclear use would 'cross a line that the international community has drawn together' (AP, 22). That line is the TPNW, whose Article 1(1)(d) bans states to 'use or threaten to use' nuclear weapons (TPNW Text, 17).

prefires.chip: S18. Doesn't the TPNW Help Putin?
prefires.topicLabel: Isn't the TPNW exactly what Putin wants, a disarmed West?
prefires.coreAnswer: Putin is not on the TPNW's side: the nuclear-weapon states, Russia included, boycotted the 2017 negotiations (ACA, 25), no nuclear-armed state has signed, and Russia has spent this war making the very threats the treaty bans (AP, 22). A treaty that gives Europe a legal and moral argument to stop paying Rosatom about 781 million euros a year (Danylyuk, 26) is the opposite of a gift to the Kremlin.

mythPrefires.topicLabel: Aren't Russia and China NATO members?
mythPrefires.coreAnswer: That's simply not true: Russia and China are not NATO members. NATO's own website says 'At present, NATO has 32 member countries,' and neither Russia nor China is on the list (NATO Member Countries, 24). In April 2014 NATO foreign ministers 'decided to suspend all practical civilian and military cooperation between NATO and Russia' (NATO Foreign Ministers, 14). Judge, you can check the 32 names yourself on nato.int.
mustContainAny: russia and china are in nato
mythPrefires.citation: NATO Member Countries, 24 & NATO Foreign Ministers, 14

mythPrefires.chip: M2. MYTH: TPNW Bans Nuclear Power
mythPrefires.topicLabel: Doesn't the TPNW ban nuclear power plants?
mythPrefires.coreAnswer: That's simply not true: the TPNW bans nuclear weapons, not nuclear power. Its preamble says 'nothing in this Treaty shall be interpreted as affecting the inalienable right of its States Parties to develop research, production and use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes without discrimination' (TPNW Text, 17). France could keep every reactor it runs today.

mythPrefires.topicLabel: Doesn't the TPNW force Britain and France to disarm overnight?
mythPrefires.coreAnswer: That's simply not true: TPNW states parties set 'a maximum upper limit of 10 years' to destroy weapons, plus 'a maximum extension period of up to five years' (TPNW 1MSP Decision 1, 22), under a verified, time-bound plan. To be precise, Article 4 does require weapons to come off operational status immediately and hosted bombs to leave within 90 days, but destruction is a decade-long verified process, not overnight.

mythPrefires.chip: M4. MYTH: NATO Members Already Joined
mythPrefires.topicLabel: Haven't some NATO members already joined the TPNW?
mythPrefires.coreAnswer: That's simply not true: no NATO member has signed or ratified the TPNW, which is exactly why this resolution asks whether they should. The Netherlands was the only NATO state in the 2017 negotiations and it 'voted against adoption' (ACA, 25), and none of the 32 appears among the 75 states parties (Hiroshima TPNW Tracker, 26).

mythPrefires.chip: M5. MYTH: Ukraine Was in NATO
mythPrefires.topicLabel: Wasn't Ukraine a NATO member when Russia invaded?
mythPrefires.coreAnswer: That's simply not true: Ukraine has never been a NATO member. It is not among NATO's 32 member countries listed on nato.int (NATO Member Countries, 24), so it had no Article 5 guarantee when Russia invaded in 2014 and 2022. That's the point: Russia attacked the country outside the alliance, not the allies inside it.

mythPrefires.topicLabel: Doesn't ratifying the TPNW mean leaving NATO?
mythPrefires.coreAnswer: That's simply not true: Harvard Law School's clinic concludes a TPNW member can stay in NATO and take part in joint operations, as long as it gives up the nuclear umbrella and doesn't assist banned activities (Harvard Law Clinic, 18). NATO's founding treaty 'does not mention nuclear weapons' (Hill, 21), and nothing in it expels a member.

mythPrefires.chip: M7. MYTH: Russia or US Signed
mythPrefires.topicLabel: Didn't Russia or the United States sign the TPNW?
mythPrefires.coreAnswer: That's simply not true: no nuclear-armed state has signed the TPNW. Washington and the other nuclear-weapon states 'boycotted the working group sessions and the 2017 treaty negotiations' (ACA, 25), and none appears on the UN list of signatories and parties (Hiroshima TPNW Tracker, 26). That's why our case runs through European law, not Russian promises.

mythPrefires.chip: M8. MYTH: No Country Supports It
mythPrefires.topicLabel: Doesn't almost no country support the TPNW?
mythPrefires.coreAnswer: That's simply not true: 122 countries voted to adopt the TPNW in 2017 (ACA, 25), and as of September 23, 2026 it had 75 states parties and 101 countries that had signed or joined (Hiroshima TPNW Tracker, 26). What it lacks is the nuclear-armed states, and that is the whole debate.

mythPrefires.chip: M9. MYTH: NPT Already Bans Nukes
mythPrefires.topicLabel: Doesn't the NPT already ban nuclear weapons?
mythPrefires.coreAnswer: That's simply not true: the NPT lets five states keep nuclear weapons and only asks them to 'pursue negotiations in good faith' toward disarmament (NPT Text, 68, Article VI). It never bans the weapons themselves. The TPNW is the first treaty that does, which is why it's the 'effective measure' Article VI calls for.

mythPrefires.topicLabel: Doesn't Europe have no real military without nukes?
mythPrefires.coreAnswer: That's simply not true: the 29 European NATO members spent $559 billion on their militaries in 2025, nearly three times Russia's $190 billion, and their spending 'rose faster than at any time since 1953' (SIPRI, 26). Germany alone spent $114 billion. Europe has a huge conventional military; the TPNW only takes away the bombs.

shieldSnippets.label: Shield 1. No New Arguments in Final Focus (NSDA Ballot)
shieldSnippets.text: Judge, the NSDA Public Forum ballot says: 'No new arguments may be introduced in the Final Focus; however, debaters may include new evidence to support prior arguments.' Because we speak first, our opponents get the last word. If their Final Focus raises an argument we never heard in their earlier speeches, please leave it off your flow, because we never had a chance to answer it.

shieldSnippets.label: Shield 2. Check the Card, Not the Claim
shieldSnippets.text: Judge, if their last speech states a 'fact' you didn't hear earlier, like Russia or China being in NATO, ask: did they read a source for it, and did we get to answer it? Every number we gave you has a named source we can show you. NATO's own website lists 32 members, and Russia and China are not among them. Please vote on what was proven in the round, not on claims made where no one could respond.

shieldSnippets.label: Shield 3. The Three-Question Flow Test
shieldSnippets.text: Judge, here's a simple test for their Final Focus. For each reason they give you, ask three questions: Was it in their Summary? Did they read a source for it? Did we get a chance to answer it? If any answer is no, it shouldn't decide the round. It's a standard debate norm that the last speeches extend what's already on the flow. Our contentions were extended in our Summary, with sources, and they answered every Con argument.

sourceCards.title: Statement by the North Atlantic Council on the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty
sourceCards.citation: North Atlantic Council (NATO), August 2, 2019.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: NATO itself found Russia violated the INF Treaty with the 9M729 missile while NATO's nuclear deterrent was fully in place.
sourceCards.verbatim: “Russia today remains in violation of the INF Treaty, despite years of U.S. and Allied engagement, including a final opportunity over six months to honour its Treaty obligations.” … “Russia bears sole responsibility for the demise of the Treaty.” … “NATO will respond in a measured and responsible way to the significant risks posed by the Russian 9M729 missile to Allied security.”

sourceCards.title: Russia Suspends New START
sourceCards.citation: Shannon Bugos, Arms Control Today (Arms Control Association), March 2023.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: Putin suspended the last US-Russia nuclear arms treaty in February 2023.
sourceCards.verbatim: “I am compelled to announce today that Russia is suspending its participation” in New START, Putin said in a state-of-the-nation address to the Federal Assembly on Feb. 21.

sourceCards.title: Putin signs bill revoking Russia's ratification of a global nuclear test ban treaty
sourceCards.citation: Associated Press via PBS NewsHour, November 2, 2023.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: Russia walked back its test-ban ratification. Counter: Moscow says it only 'mirrors' the US, which signed but never ratified the CTBT.
sourceCards.verbatim: “President Vladimir Putin on Thursday signed a bill revoking Russia's ratification of a global nuclear test ban, a move that Moscow said was needed to establish parity with the United States.”

sourceCards.title: New START Expires As U.S. Urges ‘Modernized’ Treaty
sourceCards.citation: Xiaodon Liang, Arms Control Today, March 2026.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: bilateral arms control is gone. Honest note: the US did not respond to Russia's offer to keep the limits informally.
sourceCards.verbatim: “The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) expired Feb. 5 without a U.S. response to a Russian offer to continue informally abiding by the central limits of the agreement, leaving the two nuclear superpowers with no legally binding curbs on deploying their strategic weapon.” Also: “China will not take part in nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage,” Shen Jian said Feb. 6.

sourceCards.title: Russian President Putin signs a new doctrine that lowers the threshold for using nuclear weapons
sourceCards.citation: Associated Press (via Canadian Press / CFJC Today), November 19, 2024.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: Russia lowered its nuclear threshold while NATO's full deterrent was in place.
sourceCards.verbatim: “Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday signed a revised nuclear doctrine declaring that a conventional attack on Russia by any nation that is supported by a nuclear power will be considered a joint attack on his country.”

sourceCards.title: Putin says Russia tested a new intermediate-range ballistic missile on Ukraine
sourceCards.citation: Polina Lytvynova, Hanna Palamarenko and Charles Maynes, NPR, November 21, 2024.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: Russia fired its new nuclear-capable missile at Dnipro with about 100 US B61s already in Europe; it carried a conventional warhead.
sourceCards.verbatim: “Russia fired an experimental intermediate-range ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Russian President Vladimir Putin said in a TV speech Thursday, warning that the Kremlin could use it against military installations of countries that have allowed Ukraine to use their missiles to strike inside Russia. Putin said the new missile, called “Oreshnik,” Russian for “hazel,” used a nonnuclear warhead.”

sourceCards.title: Russia uses its new hypersonic missile in major attack on Ukraine and warning to the West
sourceCards.citation: Samya Kullab and Illia Novikov, Associated Press via PBS NewsHour, January 9, 2026.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: a second Oreshnik launch near the Polish border, aimed as a warning to NATO, again undeterred by NATO nukes.
sourceCards.verbatim: “For only the second time in the nearly 4-year-old war, it used a powerful, new hypersonic missile that struck western Ukraine in a clear warning to Kyiv's NATO allies.” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the Oreshnik launch was “meant as a warning to Europe and to the U.S.”

sourceCards.title: Russia deploys hypersonic Oreshnik missiles in Belarus amid Europe tensions
sourceCards.citation: David D. Lee and Reuters, Al Jazeera, December 31, 2025.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: Russia moved Oreshnik into Belarus with NATO's B61s in place, so the bombs did not deter the deployment.
sourceCards.verbatim: “The Russian Oreshnik missile systems entered combat duty in [Belarus].” (Russian Ambassador Boris Gryzlov, via TASS) Also: “Analysts note that stationing the Oreshnik missiles in Belarus could shorten the time for Russian nuclear weapons to reach European targets.”

sourceCards.title: Putin puts Russia's nuclear forces on alert, cites sanctions
sourceCards.citation: Associated Press via WITF, February 27, 2022.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: Russian nuclear blackmail began with NATO's full deterrent in place.
sourceCards.verbatim: “Putin ordered the Russian defense minister and the chief of the military’s General Staff to put the nuclear deterrent forces in a “special regime of combat duty.””

sourceCards.title: Cornered by war, Putin makes another nuclear threat
sourceCards.citation: Associated Press via News4Jax, September 21, 2022.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: Putin's threats kept coming; deterrence did not stop them.
sourceCards.verbatim: “In a televised address to the nation Wednesday, Putin said Moscow's nuclear arsenal is more modern than NATO's and declared his readiness to use them. “This is not a bluff,” Putin added somberly…”

sourceCards.title: China's Xi says international community should oppose threat of nuclear weapon use
sourceCards.citation: Associated Press via KATV, November 4, 2022.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: the global norm against nuclear threats, which the TPNW codifies, was used to pressure Russia.
sourceCards.verbatim: The international community should “create conditions for the resumption of negotiations (and) jointly oppose the use or threat of use of nuclear weapons,” Xi said. Scholz: “President Xi and I agree that nuclear threats are irresponsible and highly dangerous. By using nuclear weapons, Russia would cross a line that the international community has drawn together.”

sourceCards.title: Global Britain in a Competitive Age: the Integrated Review of Security, Defence, Development and Foreign Policy
sourceCards.citation: HM Government (UK), March 16, 2021.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: the UK reversed its planned cut and raised its warhead ceiling, and cut transparency. Note: the UK says 180 was a goal, not a cap; the previous cap was 225.
sourceCards.verbatim: “In 2010 the Government stated an intent to reduce our overall nuclear warhead stockpile ceiling from not more than 225 to not more than 180 by the mid-2020s. However, in recognition of the evolving security environment, including the developing range of technological and doctrinal threats, this is no longer possible, and the UK will move to an overall nuclear weapon stockpile of no more than 260 warheads.” … “we will … no longer give public figures for our operational stockpile, deployed warhead or deployed missile numbers.”

sourceCards.title: Visit to the Île Longue Operational Base (forward deterrence speech)
sourceCards.citation: President Emmanuel Macron, official English text, Élysée, March 2, 2026.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: France is adding warheads and hiding numbers, and its 'forward deterrence' carries no guarantee and no shared decision. Note: Macron frames it as an addition to NATO's nuclear mission.
sourceCards.verbatim: “I prefer to be clear from the start, there will be no sharing of the ultimate decision, nor of its planification, nor of its conduct.” … “there will also be no sharing of the definition of our vital interests, which will remain of sovereign assessment for our country. And for this reason, as with other nuclear alliances, including when they have plans and procedures, there will be no guarantee in the strict sense of the term.” … “I have decided to increase the number of warheads of our arsenal. To put an end to any speculation, we will no longer release figures on our nuclear arsenal, as we have done in the past.”

sourceCards.title: Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (text)
sourceCards.citation: Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, opened for signature July 1, 1968 (UN text).
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: the NPT does not ban the weapons; Article VI only requires good-faith negotiations, and Article II bars non-nuclear states from acquiring bombs.
sourceCards.verbatim: Article VI: “Each of the Parties to the Treaty undertakes to pursue negotiations in good faith on effective measures relating to cessation of the nuclear arms race at an early date and to nuclear disarmament, and on a treaty on general and complete disarmament under strict and effective international control.” Article II: “Each non-nuclear-weapon State Party to the Treaty undertakes … not to manufacture or otherwise acquire nuclear weapons or other nuclear explosive devices…”

sourceCards.title: Increasing focus on nuclear weapons amid heightened escalation risks: new SIPRI Yearbook out now
sourceCards.citation: Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, press release, June 8, 2026.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: deterrence-led policies are fuelling an arms race; China grows fastest; the UK and France are expanding or less transparent. Note: China's growth slowed (about +20 in the last year).
sourceCards.verbatim: “SIPRI estimates that China now has around 620 nuclear warheads. China is expanding its nuclear arsenal faster than any other country…” “Yet even if China surpasses 1000 warheads by 2030, that will still amount to only about one quarter of each of the current Russian and US nuclear stockpiles.” Kristensen: “The evidence is growing that the nuclear weapon states are sidelining, and even walking away from, their disarmament commitments and are instead flexing their nuclear muscles… By reaching for nuclear solutions, states are creating new risks and fuelling arms-race dynamics.” Haggag: “making national defence and security strategies dependent—or more dependent—on nuclear weapons could significantly increase nuclear risks.”

sourceCards.title: China’s military buildup makes US increasingly vulnerable, DOD says
sourceCards.citation: Defense News, December 24, 2025, reporting the Pentagon's 2025 China Military Power Report. (The 2020 report's 'low 200s' estimate was widely reported, e.g. Defense News, Sept 1, 2020.)
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: China's arsenal kept growing despite US deterrence.
sourceCards.verbatim: “And while China’s stockpile of nuclear warheads remained in the “low 600s” at the end of 2024, “reflecting a slower rate of production when compared to previous years,” Beijing is on track to surpass 1,000 warheads by 2030, according to the report.”

sourceCards.title: Trump orders the Pentagon to immediately resume testing U.S. nuclear weapons after a gap of 33 years
sourceCards.citation: Trevor Hunnicutt, Ismail Shakil and Kanishka Singh, Reuters (via Philadelphia Inquirer), October 30, 2025.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: the umbrella-holder itself talked of resuming tests. Counter: Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Nov 2, 2025 that the tests would not be nuclear explosions (Summary, not a quote).
sourceCards.verbatim: “Because of other countries testing programs, I have instructed the Department of War to start testing our Nuclear Weapons on an equal basis. That process will begin immediately,” President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social.

sourceCards.title: NATO presses ahead with Steadfast Noon nuclear drill after Russia's nuclear warning
sourceCards.citation: Associated Press via News4Jax, October 8, 2026.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: Russian nuclear threats and NATO nuclear drills feed each other.
sourceCards.verbatim: “NATO will hold its major annual nuclear exercise next week, senior officials at the military alliance said on Thursday, just weeks after Russia warned that it would not hesitate to use nuclear weapons should its territory come under threat.” Russian embassy statement: “There should be no mistake – Russia would be ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate the Kaliningrad region from the rest of the country.” NATO's Nassima Barrows: “Our exercise Steadfast Noon is routine.”

sourceCards.title: NATO begins annual nuclear exercise in Italy
sourceCards.citation: John Vandiver, Stars and Stripes, October 13, 2026.
sourceCards.takeaway: Dates and scale of Steadfast Noon 2026.
sourceCards.verbatim: “NATO’s annual Steadfast Noon nuclear exercise runs Oct. 13-23 in Italy, with 17 nations participating.”

sourceCards.title: NATO 2022 Strategic Concept
sourceCards.citation: NATO, adopted at the Madrid Summit, June 29, 2022.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: NATO defines itself as a nuclear alliance, so its statements on the TPNW come from an interested party.
sourceCards.verbatim: “The fundamental purpose of NATO’s nuclear capability is to preserve peace, prevent coercion and deter aggression. As long as nuclear weapons exist, NATO will remain a nuclear alliance. NATO’s goal is a safer world for all; we seek to create the security environment for a world without nuclear weapons.”

sourceCards.title: Statement by NATO Foreign Ministers
sourceCards.citation: NATO Foreign Ministers, Brussels, April 1, 2014 (published on GOV.UK).
sourceCards.takeaway: Myth-buster: Russia is not a NATO partner, let alone a member.
sourceCards.verbatim: “We have decided to suspend all practical civilian and military cooperation between NATO and Russia.”

sourceCards.title: NATO member countries
sourceCards.citation: NATO, official website, page updated March 11, 2024.
sourceCards.takeaway: Myth-buster: 32 members; Russia, China and Ukraine are not among them.
sourceCards.verbatim: “At present, NATO has 32 member countries.” … “NATO was created by 12 countries from Europe and North America on 4 April 1949.” “Since then, 20 more countries have joined NATO through 10 rounds of enlargement (in 1952, 1955, 1982, 1999, 2004, 2009, 2017, 2020, 2023 and 2024).”

sourceCards.title: Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (certified true copy)
sourceCards.citation: Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons, adopted July 7, 2017; in force January 22, 2021 (UN Treaty Collection).
sourceCards.takeaway: Myth-buster: protects peaceful nuclear energy; bans use and threats.
sourceCards.verbatim: Preamble: “Emphasizing that nothing in this Treaty shall be interpreted as affecting the inalienable right of its States Parties to develop research, production and use of nuclear energy for peaceful purposes without discrimination,” Article 1(1): “Each State Party undertakes never under any circumstances to: … (d) Use or threaten to use nuclear weapons or other nuclear explosive devices;”

sourceCards.title: Report of the first Meeting of States Parties to the TPNW (TPNW/MSP/2022/6), Annex III, Decision 1
sourceCards.citation: First Meeting of States Parties, Vienna, decision adopted June 22, 2022.
sourceCards.takeaway: Myth-buster: destruction is up to 10 years plus up to 5, not overnight. Honest note: host states must remove foreign weapons within 90 days.
sourceCards.verbatim: “(a) To adopt a maximum upper limit of 10 years as the deadline required for nuclear weapons destruction…” “(b) To establish a maximum extension period of up to five years for the destruction of nuclear weapons;” “(h) To adopt a deadline of up to a maximum period of 90 days for the removal of nuclear weapons from hosting States.”

sourceCards.title: Status of the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons
sourceCards.citation: Hiroshima Prefecture (Hiroshima for Global Peace), based on UN data, as of September 23, 2026.
sourceCards.takeaway: Myth-buster: 75 states parties; 101 countries have signed or joined; no NATO member and no nuclear-armed state.
sourceCards.verbatim: “(As of September 23, 2026) Signatory Countries/Regions: 96 (Signatory only 26) Ratifying Countries/Regions: 75 (Including 5 Accession)”

sourceCards.title: The Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons At A Glance
sourceCards.citation: Arms Control Association fact sheet (status line dated September 24, 2025).
sourceCards.takeaway: Myth-buster: 122 states adopted the treaty; nuclear-weapon states boycotted.
sourceCards.verbatim: “…participants adopting the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons by a vote of 122-1-1. The Netherlands voted against adoption, and Singapore abstained.” “…leaders from Washington and the other nuclear-weapon states boycotted the working group sessions and the 2017 treaty negotiations.”

sourceCards.title: Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany
sourceCards.citation: Treaty on the Final Settlement with Respect to Germany, signed Moscow, September 12, 1990, Article 3(1).
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: Germany is legally committed never to have nuclear weapons.
sourceCards.verbatim: “The Governments of the Federal Republic of Germany and the German Democratic Republic reaffirm their renunciation of the manufacture and possession of and control over nuclear, biological and chemical weapons. They declare that the united Germany, too, will abide by these commitments.”

sourceCards.title: 22 U.S. Code § 1928f: Limitation on withdrawal from the North Atlantic Treaty Organization
sourceCards.citation: Section 1250A, National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024 (Dec 2023), codified at 22 U.S.C. § 1928f (Cornell LII).
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: Trump cannot legally quit NATO alone; Europe keeps the Article 5 alliance.
sourceCards.verbatim: “The President shall not suspend, terminate, denounce, or withdraw the United States from the North Atlantic Treaty, done at Washington, DC, April 4, 1949, except by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, provided that two-thirds of the Senators present concur, or pursuant to an Act of Congress.”

sourceCards.title: Trump casts doubt on NATO solidarity, despite it aiding the US after Sept. 11
sourceCards.citation: Michelle L. Price, Associated Press via News4Jax, March 6, 2025.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: the sitting president made defense conditional on payment.
sourceCards.verbatim: “Well, I think it’s common sense, right? If they don’t pay, I’m not going to defend them. No, I’m not going to defend them.”

sourceCards.title: Trump says whether he'll commit to NATO mutual defense guarantee 'depends on your definition'
sourceCards.citation: Molly Quell, Lorne Cook and Mike Corder, Associated Press via ABC7, June 24, 2025.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: the US commitment to Article 5 is openly conditional. Counter: at the summit he later said the US was with allies.
sourceCards.verbatim: “Depends on your definition,” Trump told reporters as he was headed to The Hague… “There's numerous definitions of Article 5. You know that, right? But I'm committed to being their friends.”

sourceCards.title: National Security Strategy of the United States of America (November 2025)
sourceCards.citation: The White House, released December 4, 2025.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: US strategy tells Europe to defend itself and doubts allies' reliability. Counter: it also promises a credible deterrent that protects allies.
sourceCards.verbatim: “it is far from obvious whether certain European countries will have economies and militaries strong enough to remain reliable allies.” “Enabling Europe to stand on its own feet and operate as a group of aligned sovereign nations, including by taking primary responsibility for its own defense”

sourceCards.title: Trump says the U.S. will reduce number of troops in Germany 'a lot further' than withdrawal of 5,000
sourceCards.citation: CNBC, May 2, 2026.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: US forces in Europe are being pulled back; the gap is conventional.
sourceCards.verbatim: “We're going to cut way down. And we're cutting a lot further than 5,000,” (President Trump)

sourceCards.title: Trump says 8 European nations face tariffs rising to 25% if Greenland isn't sold to the U.S.
sourceCards.citation: Kevin Breuninger and Luke Fountain, CNBC, January 17, 2026.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: the US coerced NATO allies, so Trump's threats exist regardless of the TPNW. Counter: he dropped the tariffs on Jan 21, 2026.
sourceCards.verbatim: Trump's post: “until such time as a Deal is reached for the Complete and Total purchase of Greenland.”

sourceCards.title: Pentagon scales back troops from NATO eastern flank, denies American withdrawal from Europe
sourceCards.citation: Rachel Wolf and Jennifer Griffin, Fox News, October 29, 2025.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: eastern-flank cuts drew Republican opposition. Counter: the Army said it is not a withdrawal; about 1,000 US troops stay in Romania.
sourceCards.verbatim: Sen. Roger Wicker and Rep. Mike Rogers: “We strongly oppose the decision not to maintain the rotational U.S. brigade in Romania.” US Army: “This is not an American withdrawal from Europe or a signal of lessened commitment to NATO and Article 5.”

sourceCards.title: Home alone: Europeans are ready to defend themselves
sourceCards.citation: Jana Kobzová and Paweł Zerka, European Council on Foreign Relations, June 10, 2026 (15-country poll).
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: Europeans no longer believe the US umbrella. Counter: the same poll finds openness to a European nuclear deterrent.
sourceCards.verbatim: “majorities in every European country polled think that the US would not support them if they came under attack—whereas they do trust their European neighbours to do so.”

sourceCards.title: Speech by the Federal Chancellor at the Munich Security Conference
sourceCards.citation: Chancellor Friedrich Merz, official English transcript, February 13, 2026.
sourceCards.takeaway: PRO: Germany's own leader says the US relationship is broken, so relying on US bombs is the risk. Counter: Merz wants deterrence embedded in NATO nuclear sharing.
sourceCards.verbatim: “Allow me to start with an uncomfortable truth: a chasm, a deep rift, has opened between Europe and the United States.” Also: “We are thinking of nuclear deterrence strictly embedded in our nuclear sharing within NATO.”

sourceCards.title: Public Forum Debate Ballot (NSDA form)
sourceCards.citation: National Speech & Debate Association Public Forum ballot (copy hosted by a state forensics club; check your tournament's ballot).
sourceCards.takeaway: Shield: new arguments are barred in Final Focus.
sourceCards.verbatim: “No new arguments may be introduced in the Final Focus; however, debaters may include new evidence to support prior arguments.” Also: “Judges should decide the round as it is debated, not based on their personal beliefs.”

notes: COUNTER-EVIDENCE AND HONESTY NOTES. (1) New START: Russia suspended in Feb 2023, but at expiry (Feb 5, 2026) the US never answered Russia's offer to keep the limits informally (Liang, 26). Say both superpowers let arms control die; don't say Russia alone killed it. (2) CTBT: Russia says it 'mirrors' the US, which signed but never ratified the CTBT. (3) US testing: Energy Secretary Chris Wright said on Nov 2, 2025 the tests would not be nuclear explosions ('noncritical'); don't claim the US has tested a bomb. (4) Oreshnik: used with conventional (nonnuclear) warheads at Dnipro (Nov 2024), near Lviv (Jan 2026) and, per SIPRI, again in May 2026. Call it 'nuclear-capable', never 'a nuclear strike'. (5) China: growth slowed (SIPRI: +20 to ~620 in the last year; Pentagon: 'slower rate of production'). The 'low 200s in 2020' figure is the Pentagon's 2020 estimate, widely reported; FAS estimated about 300 then. (6) UK: the 2021 Review raised the ceiling to 260; the UK says 180 was a goal, not a cap, and the cap before was 225. Say 'abandoned its planned cut to 180 and raised the ceiling to 260.' (7) TPNW Article 4: weapons must leave operational status immediately and hosted weapons must go within 90 days (1MSP Decision 1(h)). Only destruction takes up to 10 + 5 years. Don't claim 'nothing changes for 10 years.' (8) Harvard Law Clinic, 18 also says a TPNW state must give up the nuclear umbrella. Concede that and pivot to 'the umbrella is a conditional bluff anyway.' (9) Trump counter-evidence: the July 2026 Ankara summit declaration reaffirmed an 'ironclad commitment' to Article 5; new US rotations reached Lithuania (Oct 2026) and reportedly Estonia; Trump pledged 5,000 more troops to Poland; the Romania cut left about 1,000 US troops there. Use prefire S2 ('either way we win'). (10) Forward deterrence: Macron says it adds to NATO's nuclear mission, and about 10 partners, including Finland (Sept 2026), have joined. Don't say Europe rejects it; say it carries 'no guarantee in the strict sense' by Macron's own words. (11) TPNW counts: 75 states parties and 101 countries signed or joined as of Sept 23, 2026 (Hiroshima tracker, from UN data). The first TPNW Review Conference is reportedly set for Nov 30 to Dec 4, 2026 (not verified on a UN page); re-check the counts before each tournament. (12) Shield rule: the NSDA ballot bars new ARGUMENTS in Final Focus but allows new EVIDENCE for prior arguments. 'Nothing new after Summary' is a norm, not a ballot rule; Shield 3 says so. (13) The existing card 'Brennan & Panetta, 25' (the CIA video) was not confirmed by earlier research (research_us_reliability C7). Prefer the AP Trump quotes in pro_reb_s3 and p_pf_s2. (14) Wording: Xi's 'jointly oppose' line is AP's translation of Chinese state TV (CCTV). Steadfast Noon: 'Russia's nuclear rhetoric is on the rise' is AP's paraphrase of NATO's Barrows, not her quote. (15) The Belarus 'B61s gave Putin an excuse' card (Al Jazeera, 23) and 'about 100 B61s' (Kristensen, 26) are existing app cards; cardKeys reuse their exact short names. New card shorts have no apostrophes ('If They Dont Pay' on purpose).
